missions/methodist-mission/name: Evangelical Revival and Methodist missions (Wesley, Whitefield, Coke, Asbury)
missions/methodist-mission/origin/name: London (Aldersgate and the Foundery) and Bristol
missions/methodist-mission/statusNote: The British and American Methodist missionary societies have been absorbed into church agencies (the Methodist Church in Britain's World Church Relationships; the United Methodist General Board of Global Ministries), and almost all former mission fields are autonomous conferences. The World Methodist Council's member churches report around 80 million people, increasingly in Africa and Asia; American United Methodism divided in 2019–24, when about a quarter of US congregations left, many joining the Global Methodist Church.
missions/methodist-mission/summary: The Evangelical Revival of the 1730s–40s, led by John and Charles Wesley and George Whitefield, created Methodism, a disciplined lay-led movement that treated 'the world as my parish'. Through itinerant preachers, class meetings and the missionary drive of Thomas Coke and Francis Asbury, Methodism spread across the American frontier, the Caribbean, West and Southern Africa, the South Pacific, India and East Asia, becoming one of the largest Protestant families and a seedbed of the Holiness and Pentecostal movements.
missions/methodist-mission/story:
The revival grew from the 'Holy Club' at Oxford, where from 1729 John and Charles Wesley, George Whitefield and others pursued disciplined piety. John Wesley's failed mission as an SPG chaplain in Georgia (1735–37), where he met Moravian missionaries on the voyage, preceded his experience at a society meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738, when he felt his heart 'strangely warmed'. Whitefield, a spellbinding preacher, began open-air preaching to the miners of Kingswood near Bristol in February 1739 and persuaded Wesley to follow. Wesley declared in 1739 that he looked upon 'all the world as my parish', and for fifty years he rode some 250,000 miles organising societies, classes and bands across Britain and Ireland.

Whitefield crossed the Atlantic seven times and became the best-known figure of the Great Awakening in the American colonies, preaching from Georgia to New England in 1739–40 to crowds that sometimes reached tens of thousands; he died at Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1770. Methodism proper reached America through Irish immigrants, Philip Embury and Barbara Heck in New York (1766) and Robert Strawbridge in Maryland. Wesley sent preachers from 1769, including Francis Asbury (1771), who stayed through the Revolution. After American independence Wesley ordained Thomas Coke as superintendent, and at the Christmas Conference in Baltimore in December 1784 the Methodist Episcopal Church was organised with Coke and Asbury as its superintendents (soon styled bishops). Circuit riders carried Methodism to the frontier, and by 1830 it was the largest denomination in the United States.

Coke, a Welsh Anglican clergyman, was Methodism's missionary strategist. His 1783–84 Plan of the Society for the Establishment of Missions among the Heathens anticipated Carey's Enquiry. In 1786, bound for Nova Scotia, his ship was driven by storms to Antigua, where he landed on Christmas Day; there the planter Nathaniel Gilbert had begun preaching to his slaves in 1759, enslaved women such as Sophia Campbell and Mary Alley had kept the society going, and the shipwright John Baxter was leading some 2,000 members. Coke left missionaries across the Caribbean, crossed the Atlantic eighteen times, and in 1813 persuaded the Conference to launch a mission to Asia. He died at sea on 3 May 1814; his companions landed in Bombay and established the Ceylon mission.

The Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society, formed in 1813–18, became one of the largest British societies. Sierra Leone (1811) built on Black Loyalist Methodists who had settled there from Nova Scotia in 1792; Barnabas Shaw entered South Africa in 1816 and William Shaw led the mission among the Xhosa from 1823. Thomas Birch Freeman, the son of an African father and English mother, reached Kumasi in Asante in 1839 and Badagry and Abeokuta in Yorubaland in 1842. In the Pacific, Tonga (1822, firmly from 1826) became Methodist after the baptism of Taufa'ahau, later King George Tupou I, in 1831, and Fiji (1835) followed, with the chief Cakobau converting in 1854 and Tongan and Fijian teachers carrying the faith further to Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. Missions also went to Madras (1817), China (1851) and later to Burma and Upper Burma.

American Methodism created its own Missionary Society in 1819. Melville Cox died within months of landing in Liberia in 1833 ('Let a thousand fall before Africa be given up'); William Butler began the North India mission at Bareilly in 1856, where Isabella Thoburn later founded the school that became Lucknow's Isabella Thoburn College; and Henry Appenzeller entered Korea in 1885. Black Methodist churches formed in protest at discrimination: the African Methodist Episcopal Church under Richard Allen (1816), which sent missionaries to Haiti, Sierra Leone and Liberia and in 1896 absorbed South Africa's Ethiopian Church, and the AME Zion Church.

Methodism repeatedly divided. Whitefield's Calvinist Methodists separated from Wesley's Arminians in 1741; British Methodism fractured into the Methodist New Connexion (1797), Primitive Methodists (1811), Bible Christians (1815) and others, each with missions, before reuniting in 1932. American Methodists split North and South over slavery in 1844 and reunited in 1939 (without the Black churches); the United Methodist Church was formed in 1968. Methodist teaching on Christian perfection fed the nineteenth-century Holiness movement and, through it, Pentecostalism, while Methodists such as John R. Mott were leading architects of the ecumenical movement. Former mission districts became autonomous conferences from the late nineteenth century onward, and today the churches of Africa, Asia, the Pacific and Latin America form the growing part of world Methodism.
missions/methodist-mission/beliefs/0: Arminian evangelical theology: Christ died for all, prevenient grace enables every person to respond, and 'all may be saved'.
missions/methodist-mission/beliefs/1: The new birth and the witness of the Spirit, giving believers an assurance of salvation.
missions/methodist-mission/beliefs/2: Christian perfection or entire sanctification: the possibility of perfect love toward God and neighbour in this life.
missions/methodist-mission/beliefs/3: Social holiness: faith expressed in disciplined community and works of mercy, including Wesley's opposition to slavery (Thoughts upon Slavery, 1774) and to gin and smuggling.
missions/methodist-mission/beliefs/4: The use of the 'means of grace' (prayer, Scripture, the Lord's Supper, fasting, Christian conference) as ordinary channels of God's grace.
missions/methodist-mission/beliefs/5: A sense of urgency that the gospel should be offered to everyone, everywhere, expressed in Wesley's 'the world is my parish'.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/0: Field preaching and itinerancy: preachers on horseback 'riding the circuit', from British market towns to the American frontier.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/1: Class meetings of about twelve under a lay leader, bands and quarterly tickets, which gave converts discipline and pastoral care and let laypeople, including women and enslaved people, lead.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/2: Lay preachers, local preachers and exhorters, including Black and women preachers in the early decades.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/3: Hymn-singing: Charles Wesley's roughly 6,000 hymns carried theology to people who could not read.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/4: Connexional organisation: an annual Conference that stationed preachers and directed resources across vast distances, adapted to mission districts overseas.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/5: Schools, printing and later hospitals and colleges, especially in India, Africa, Korea and China.
missions/methodist-mission/strategies/6: Use of indigenous evangelists, notably Tongan and Fijian missionaries who carried Methodism across Melanesia.
missions/methodist-mission/groupsReached: Industrial workers, miners and the rural poor of Britain and Ireland.
Settlers and enslaved and free African Americans in North America, including the frontier and the slave South.
Enslaved and free people of colour in Antigua, the West Indies and Sierra Leone.
Fante and Asante in the Gold Coast, Yoruba and Egba in Nigeria, Xhosa, Mfengu and Sotho-Tswana in Southern Africa.
Tongans, Fijians and Samoans, and through Pacific teachers the peoples of New Britain, Papua and the Solomon Islands.
Tamil and Sinhala communities in Ceylon and South India, Hindi-speaking villages in North India, and Koreans, Chinese and Burmese.
missions/methodist-mission/challenges/0: Mob violence and clerical opposition in Britain in the 1740s, and hostility from planters in the Caribbean who feared Methodist preaching to the enslaved.
missions/methodist-mission/challenges/1: Tropical disease: West Africa was known as 'the white man's grave', and many early missionaries to Sierra Leone and the Gold Coast died within a year.
missions/methodist-mission/challenges/2: Tension between the Church of England and the Methodist societies, which led to separation after Wesley's death in 1791.
missions/methodist-mission/challenges/3: Slavery, which divided American Methodism in 1844 and compromised its early anti-slavery stance.
missions/methodist-mission/challenges/4: Repeated schisms over church government, lay rights and holiness teaching.
missions/methodist-mission/challenges/5: Theological liberalism and secularisation in the twentieth century, contributing to sharp decline in Britain and North America.
missions/methodist-mission/harms/0: Whitefield campaigned for the legalisation of slavery in Georgia (achieved in 1751) and owned enslaved people at his Bethesda orphanage.
missions/methodist-mission/harms/1: American Methodism retreated from Wesley's anti-slavery rules, and Southern Methodism defended slavery and later segregation; Black Methodists were pushed into separate galleries and conferences.
missions/methodist-mission/harms/2: Methodist missionaries in Fiji and Tonga were closely tied to chiefly power, and royal conversions brought coercive pressure on subjects.
missions/methodist-mission/harms/3: Some missionaries endorsed colonial expansion, such as Wesleyans who supported British annexations in the Eastern Cape and Fiji (1874).
missions/methodist-mission/harms/4: In Canada, Methodists ran Indian residential schools (later in the United Church of Canada), part of a system now recognised as causing grave harm to Indigenous children.
missions/methodist-mission/harms/5: Paternalism in mission districts delayed autonomy for African and Asian churches well into the twentieth century.
missions/methodist-mission/developments/: A mass lay movement that gave working people, women and Black Christians roles as leaders and preachers.
Charles Wesley's hymns and a congregational singing tradition now used across Protestantism.
Major contributions to education: Methodist schools and colleges across Africa, India and Korea, including Ewha (1886) and Isabella Thoburn College (1886).
Black church independence through the AME and AME Zion churches, central to African American religious and civil life.
Holiness teaching that gave rise to the Holiness churches, the Salvation Army and, indirectly, Pentecostalism.
Leadership in the ecumenical movement and social reform, including temperance, anti-slavery and later civil-rights activism.
missions/methodist-mission/outcome: From a revival within the Church of England, Methodism became a worldwide family of churches of about 80 million people. Its mission societies have been absorbed into church agencies and its overseas districts are autonomous churches, many of them growing while Western Methodism declines and divides.
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/0/f: Itinerant preaching, organising societies and classes, ordaining Coke for America
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/0/o: Left a connexion of about 72,000 members in Britain and some 57,000 in America at his death
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/1/o: His hymns became the theology of the Methodist people
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/2/f: Open-air preaching in Britain and seven American tours
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/2/o: Died at Newburyport; led the Calvinistic Methodists and supported slavery in Georgia
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/3/r: First Methodist bishop and missionary statesman
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/3/f: Organising American Methodism and missions to the West Indies, West Africa and Asia
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/3/o: Died at sea in the Indian Ocean leading the first mission to Ceylon
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/4/r: Bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/4/f: Riding some 270,000 miles to organise American Methodism
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/4/o: Methodist membership in the US grew from under 1,000 in 1771 to over 200,000 in 1816
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/5/r: Missionary in the Gold Coast and Nigeria
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/5/f: Founding Methodist work in Kumasi (1839), Badagry and Abeokuta (1842)
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/5/o: Lived the rest of his life in the Gold Coast, latterly as a Methodist minister in Accra
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/6/o: Died in Fiji; his work prepared for Cakobau's conversion in 1854
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/7/r: Pioneer of women's education in India
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/7/f: Founding a girls' school in Lucknow (1870) that became Isabella Thoburn College
missions/methodist-mission/keyPeople/7/o: First missionary of the Woman's Foreign Missionary Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church
missions/methodist-mission/countries/0/t: Field preaching, societies and classes created a mass revival movement; Methodists separated from the Church of England after 1795.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/1/t: From New York and Maryland societies to the Methodist Episcopal Church (1784), the largest US denomination by 1830, plus the AME and AME Zion churches.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/2/t: Nathaniel Gilbert's preaching and Coke's 1786 landing launched Methodist missions to enslaved people across the British Caribbean.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/3/t: Black Loyalist Methodists from Nova Scotia founded congregations in Freetown; WMMS missionaries followed in 1811.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/4/t: Coke's party established missions at Jaffna, Galle, Matara and Colombo, with Tamil and Sinhala schools.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/5/t: Barnabas Shaw in Namaqualand and William Shaw's chain of stations in the Eastern Cape; Methodism became one of South Africa's largest churches.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/6/t: After the conversion of Taufa'ahau (George Tupou I) Tonga became a largely Methodist kingdom, later with the Free Church of Tonga.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/7/t: Joseph Dunwell (1835) and Thomas Birch Freeman founded the Fante Methodist church at Cape Coast and work in Kumasi.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/8/t: Cross and Cargill landed at Lakeba; Cakobau's conversion in 1854 made Methodism the majority faith of indigenous Fijians.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/9/t: Freeman's visits to Badagry and Abeokuta began Methodist work among the Yoruba and Egba.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/10/: American Methodist mission from Melville Cox onward among Americo-Liberians and later inland peoples.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/11/: British Wesleyans in Madras, Mysore and Hyderabad; the American Methodist Episcopal mission from Bareilly (1856) grew through North Indian mass movements.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/12/: American Methodists at Fuzhou (1847) and British Wesleyans in Guangdong (1851) and Hubei.
missions/methodist-mission/countries/13/: Henry Appenzeller and Mary Scranton founded Paichai and Ewha schools in Seoul; the Korean Methodist Church became autonomous in 1930.
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/0/ti: John and Charles Wesley's voyage to Georgia (1735–1736)
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/0/pe: John and Charles Wesley, Benjamin Ingham and Charles Delamotte, with Moravian emigrants
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/0/te: On the Simmonds the Wesleys sailed with 26 Moravians led by David Nitschmann; their calm singing during an Atlantic storm convinced John Wesley that he lacked their faith. His ministry in Savannah ended in controversy and he returned to England in 1737.
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/1/te: Whitefield's tour from the middle colonies to Georgia and, in autumn 1740, through New England, where he preached in Jonathan Edwards's pulpit, drew crowds of thousands and turned local revivals into the intercolonial Great Awakening. Benjamin Franklin printed his sermons and journals.
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/2/ti: Thomas Coke's storm-driven voyage to the West Indies (1786–1787)
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/2/pe: Thomas Coke with William Warrener, William Hammet and John Clarke
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/2/te: Bound for Nova Scotia, Coke's ship was blown south and landed at Antigua on Christmas Day 1786. He left Warrener in Antigua, Clarke in St Vincent and Hammet in St Kitts, then sailed on to the American Methodist conference.
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/3/ti: Coke's last voyage and the Ceylon mission (1813–1814)
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/3/pe: Thomas Coke, James Lynch, William Ault, George Erskine, William Harvard, Thomas Squance and Benjamin Clough
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/3/te: The party sailed at the end of December 1813; Coke was found dead in his cabin on 3 May 1814 and buried at sea. The others reached Bombay and went on to Ceylon, landing at Galle in June 1814 to begin Methodist work in Asia.
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/4/ti: Thomas Birch Freeman's journeys to Kumasi and Abeokuta (1838–1842)
missions/methodist-mission/journeys/4/te: Freeman walked to the Asante capital in 1839, where the Asantehene received him, then in 1842 visited Badagry and Abeokuta at the invitation of returning Sierra Leonean Yoruba Christians, opening the Methodist Nigeria mission.
missions/methodist-mission/relations/0/t: William Booth was a Methodist New Connexion minister, and Wesleyan teaching on entire sanctification was the root of the nineteenth-century Holiness movement.
missions/methodist-mission/relations/1/t: Through the Holiness movement, Methodist perfectionism and camp-meeting revivalism fed directly into early Pentecostalism.
missions/methodist-mission/relations/2/t: American Methodists, with Presbyterians, founded Korean Protestantism from 1885, and Korean Methodists took part in the 1907 revival.
missions/methodist-mission/relations/3/t: Evangelical Anglicans who founded the CMS were products of the same Evangelical Revival, and the two movements often worked side by side.
missions/methodist-mission/agreements/0/: Both stressed assurance, small-group discipline, hymnody and early mission to the enslaved.
missions/methodist-mission/agreements/1/: Methodists such as John R. Mott were leading figures at Edinburgh 1910 and in the International Missionary Council and World Council of Churches.
missions/methodist-mission/disagreements: Wesley left the Fetter Lane Society in 1740 over Moravian 'stillness' and criticised what he saw as antinomianism in Zinzendorf.
Wesleyan Arminianism (Christ died for all) clashed with the Calvinism of Particular Baptists and of Whitefield's Calvinistic Methodists, though Carey's Fullerism narrowed the practical gap.
missions/methodist-mission/deviations/0: Wesley intended Methodism as a renewal society within the Church of England, but his ordinations for America (1784) and the Plan of Pacification (1795) made it a separate church.
missions/methodist-mission/deviations/1: American Methodism abandoned Wesley's rules against slaveholding in order to grow in the South, and the church split in 1844.
missions/methodist-mission/deviations/2: Later Methodism, especially in the West, largely abandoned the class meeting and the emphasis on entire sanctification that defined early Methodism.
